full_text:
Situation Report 
Chad Humanitarian Response 
1-31 May 2026
Highlights 
● Refugee arrivals from Sudan slow amid border insecurity: By 30 May 2026, a total of
928,818 refugees had arrived from Sudan since April 2023, with Ouaddaï hosting the largest
number.1 Arrivals declined in May, likely due to increased border insecurity, including a 26
May drone strike in Al-Tina.2
● Insecurity and funding shortfalls increase protection risks in Lac: In Lac Province,
non-state armed group (NSAG) attacks on 4 and 6 May triggered new displacements and a
state of emergency. Funding gaps have also forced humanitarian actors to scale back
services, limiting access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and protection services. A
security audit across 25 sites revealed that 96% of sites lacked night lighting and 68%
lacked latrines, heightening gender-based violence (GBV) risks.
● Intercommunal tensions restrict access to essential services in Wadi Fira: Tensions
between the Zaghawa and Tama communities persist in Wadi-Fira Province, with clashes in
Birak and Marassabré resulting in casualties. The violence undermines social cohesion,
restricts population movement, and hinders access to SRH and GBV services.
● Senior UNFPA leadership visits Chad: A high-level UNFPA mission visited N’Djamena,
Ouaddaï, and Wadi-Fira to engage with government authorities, assess humanitarian needs,
convene donor meetings, and review ongoing interventions.
● 90% funding gap: As of May 2026, UNFPA has only received 10% of funding it requires for
Chad, severely restricting life-saving SRH and GBV services for vulnerable women and girls.

related.summary: “Malnutrition remains alarmingly widespread in Kebbi State and is a leading cause of death among children under five,” says Stuart Alexander Zimble, MSF Nigeria Country Coordinator. “Authorities and humanitarian actors must urgently increase their support to prevent further avoidable deaths.” In Kebbi, an estimated 30 newborns and 100 children under the age of five die every day, with approximately 50 per cent of these deaths linked to malnutrition, according to UNICEF.
bullets: “Malnutrition remains alarmingly widespread in Kebbi State and is a leading cause of death among children under five,” says Stuart Alexander Zimble, MSF Nigeria Country Coordinator.

“Authorities and humanitarian actors must urgently increase their support to prevent further avoidable deaths.” In Kebbi, an estimated 30 newborns and 100 children under the age of five die every day, with approximately 50 per cent of these deaths linked to malnutrition, according to UNICEF.

In this initial phase, MSF will distribute about 20,000 kilograms of the locally produced flour blend in Jega and Maiyama local government areas (LGAs) to treat moderately malnourished children between six months and five years old.

Abuja, June 2026 – Following a sharp increase in cases of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) among children in Kebbi State, north‑west Nigeria, between 2024 and 2025, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has launched a nutrition initiative based on the use of Tom Brown, a locally produced complete food product designed to support children’s growth.

Despite ongoing efforts by health authorities, the needs in Kebbi remains significant, and sustained efforts by authorities, humanitarian actors and other partners are essential to improve access to healthcare and alleviate the suffering among affected communities.

related.title: Explosive Remnants of War – Lasting Harm in Deir Ez-Zor, Syria
related.summary: Today we published a report, Explosive Remnants of War – Lasting Harm in Deir ez-Zor, Syria, on the human and health impact of explosive ordnance contamination in Deir ez-Zor governorate. “For the year that we’ve been working here, we’ve seen over 215 patients suffering from blast injuries, including children and farmers working their land,” says Rebecca Kerr, MSF project coordinator in Deir ez-Zor.
bullets: Today we published a report, Explosive Remnants of War – Lasting Harm in Deir ez-Zor, Syria, on the human and health impact of explosive ordnance contamination in Deir ez-Zor governorate.

“For the year that we’ve been working here, we’ve seen over 215 patients suffering from blast injuries, including children and farmers working their land,” says Rebecca Kerr, MSF project coordinator in Deir ez-Zor.
Civilians are often injured while carrying out daily activities such as farming, herding livestock, collecting truffles, or returning to damaged homes and buildings.

Explosive ordnance continues to injure and kill people in Deir ez-Zor, Syria MSF’s latest report shares data from Deir ez-Zor, Syria, where people continue to be injured by landmines, unexploded ordnance, and abandoned explosives.

Deir ez-Zor, Syria — One year after Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) began supporting emergency services at Deir ez-Zor National hospital, in Syria, hundreds of people injured by explosive ordnance have been treated at the hospital.
related.excerpt: Explosive ordnance continues to injure and kill people in Deir ez-Zor, Syria MSF’s latest report shares data from Deir ez-Zor, Syria, where people continue to be injured by landmines, unexploded ordnance, and abandoned explosives. Over a one-year period, more than 215 injured people were treated at Deir ez-Zor National hospital. Urgent action is needed to accelerate the clearance of land contaminated by explosive ordnance and landmines, and address gaps in specialised care. Deir ez-Zor, Syria — One year after Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) began supporting emergency services at Deir ez-Zor National hospital, in Syria, hundreds of people injured by explosive ordnance have been treated at the hospital. This highlights the devastating and ongoing impact of contamination left behind by years of conflict. Today we published a report, Explosive Remnants of War – Lasting Harm in Deir ez-Zor, Syria, on the human and health impact of explosive ordnance contamination in Deir ez-Zor governorate. More than a year after the fall of the Assad government on 8 December 2024, the humanitarian situation in Syria remains challenging. Over 15.6 million people continue to require humanitarian assistance, as the consequences of 14 years of conflict, renewed instability, and prolonged neglect continue to shape daily life across the country. Civilian infrastructure has been severely weakened, with the healthcare system among the most affected sectors; MSF teams have consistently identified significant and recurrent gaps in both primary and secondary care. At the same time, explosive ordnance (EO) contamination remains one of the most serious protection risks facing civilians across Syria.
